opus-5.5.text:
I think those two things aren't actually in tension. They come from the same source.

From what's been reported, Jensen keeps a very flat structure, something like fifty or sixty direct reports, and he doesn't really do one-on-ones. He gives feedback in the open, in front of everyone, so the whole organization learns from one person's mistake. If you're one of those direct reports, that's intense. You're held to a very high bar, he's extremely detail-oriented, and there's not much room to hide. So I can completely believe people find him demanding, even hard to work with.

But popularity, both inside the company and outside, comes from something different. First, he's been right about the big bets, and he stuck with them for a very long time. CUDA is the classic example. For years Wall Street didn't understand why NVIDIA was putting so much into general-purpose GPU computing, and he kept going for more than a decade before deep learning showed up and made it obviously correct. When a leader has that kind of conviction and it pays off, people forgive a lot of intensity.

Second, he's very present. He's in the details, he works incredibly hard, and he has been with the company since the beginning, more than thirty years now. Employees can see that he isn't asking anything of them that he doesn't ask of himself. And the shareholders and employees with equity have obviously done extremely well, which helps too.

Third, as a founder myself, I've come to see that being "easy to work with" and being a great leader aren't the same thing. A CEO's job isn't to make every meeting comfortable. It's to set a clear direction, keep standards high, and make sure the company survives the hard years. Jensen has talked openly about pain and suffering being part of building character. A lot of people misread that, but I think what he means is that great things are hard, and if you protect people from all difficulty, they don't grow.

So my take is: the people closest to him feel the pressure most, but they also see the results most clearly. Many of them stay for a very long time, and I think that says more than any individual complaint.

r001.rationale: The response describes Huang’s 50–60 direct reports but never says that most NVIDIA employees do not work directly with him.

r002.rationale: It links his successful long-term bets and leadership results to employees benefiting, including noting that employees with equity have done extremely well.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key is that "hard to work with" and "popular" aren't actually in tension. They're measuring two different things.

People who report directly to Jensen describe him as demanding, blunt, sometimes brutal in meetings. He'll tear apart an idea in front of fifty people. He famously has something like fifty or sixty direct reports, no one-on-ones, and he says he does it on purpose so that information flows in public and nobody can hide. That's exhausting if you're on the receiving end. But notice what it's not. It's not political, it's not arbitrary, and it's not about him. The pressure is always pointed at the problem, not at the person's standing in the company. Engineers can tolerate a huge amount of harshness if they believe it's in service of the work and that the rules are the same for everyone.

The second piece is that he's been right, consistently, for a long time. He bet on CUDA for a decade when Wall Street thought it was a waste of money. When someone has that track record, the sharp edges get reframed as conviction rather than ego. If you're difficult and wrong, you're a tyrant. If you're difficult and right, you're a visionary. Same behavior, different label.

And the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is that he's genuinely approachable from the outside. He signs autographs on GPUs, he goes to night markets, he gives these very human commencement speeches about washing dishes and suffering. The public sees warmth and humor. The direct reports see the other side of the same intensity. Both are real.

From my own experience building a company, I'd say the lesson is not "be hard on people." The lesson is that people will follow someone demanding if the demands are consistent, if the person is clearly all-in themselves, and if the results keep showing up. Remove any one of those and the same behavior just makes you unpleasant.

astra-6.text:
I think those two things can coexist. Someone can be very inspiring as a leader and very demanding as a manager. From the outside, people see the vision, the company’s success, and the way he communicates. His direct reports experience the day-to-day pressure of trying to deliver on that vision.

I don’t know what it’s like to work directly for him, so I wouldn’t assume every account tells the whole story. But being popular isn’t the same as being easy to work with. You can respect someone’s judgment and ambition while finding the working relationship difficult. The important question is whether that pressure helps people do better work or makes it harder for them to speak honestly.
